questions.question: A batch of raw material has been made sterile by sterilizing filtration, yet the BET still detects quantifiable endotoxin activity. According to USP <1085>, what is the most reasonable explanation?

options.A: The sterilizing filtration step itself necessarily introduces new endotoxin into the raw material
options.B: After the cells die, the endotoxin in cell wall fragments can remain active, so sterile does not mean endotoxin-free
options.C: The LAL reagent used in the BET reacts only to viable Gram-negative bacteria, so this indicates viable organisms are still present
options.D: The measured activity indicates that live Gram-negative bacteria are still proliferating in the raw material, regardless of whether the cells are dead

questions.explanation: Endotoxin is a component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria and can remain active in cell wall fragments after the cell dies, so a material can be sterile and still contain quantifiable endotoxin activity. Detected endotoxin also shows that GNB growth occurred at some point in the process.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Background: Pyrogens and Endotoxins

questions.question: An injectable administered intrathecally (IT) requires an endotoxin limit calculation. According to USP <1085>, which value of K (threshold pyrogenic dose) should be used in the formula?

options.A: 5 EU/kg, the K value shared by most intravenous and non-intravenous injection routes
options.B: 100 EU/m², the K value used for parenteral products dosed per square meter of body surface area
options.C: 175 EU, the fixed K value used for intravenous radiopharmaceuticals
options.D: 0.2 EU/kg, the K value used for parenteral drugs administered intrathecally

questions.explanation: K is 5 EU/kg for most routes, but 0.2 EU/kg for parenteral products administered intrathecally, because cerebrospinal fluid is more sensitive to endotoxin and the limit is therefore stricter. 100 EU/m² and 175 EU are the values for body-surface-area dosing and intravenous radiopharmaceuticals, respectively.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Method Suitability > Calculating Endotoxin Limits for Drug and Biological Products (Table 2)

questions.question: When calibrating a new lot of CSE, the geometric mean endpoint (GM endpoint) of RSE by gel-clot is 0.125 EU/mL and that of CSE is 0.00625 ng/mL. What is the potency of the CSE, and what should be done if it is to be used with a different lot of lysate?

options.A: 20 EU/ng; changing to a different lot of lysate requires recalibration
options.B: 20 EU/ng; as long as the CSE lot is unchanged, changing the lysate lot does not require recalibration
options.C: 0.05 EU/ng; changing to a different lot of lysate requires recalibration
options.D: 0.05 EU/ng; as long as the CSE lot is unchanged, changing the lysate lot does not require recalibration

questions.explanation: Potency = GM endpoint of RSE (EU/mL) ÷ GM endpoint of CSE (ng/mL) = 0.125 ÷ 0.00625 = 20 EU/ng. The potency applies only to the specific combination of lysate lot and CSE lot, so calibration must be repeated when the lysate lot changes.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Preparatory Requirements > CSE Calibration/Potency Determination Using the Gel-Clot Method

questions.topic: Multiple populations or routes in the package insert
questions.question: A drug's package insert lists several patient populations, indications and routes of administration. How should the laboratory set the endotoxin limit specification?

options.A: Take the most lenient of the results calculated for the various conditions, so that failures are less likely in normal operation
options.B: Take the average of the results calculated for the various conditions, so that the limit falls in a reasonable middle range
options.C: Calculate separately for each administration scenario and choose the most conservative (strictest) one
options.D: Rely only on the limit already in the USP monograph, even if the laboratory's own calculation gives a lower value

questions.explanation: The chapter recommends calculating the limit separately for each administration scenario in the package insert and using the most conservative one. If the company's calculated strictest limit is lower than the USP limit, the lower in-house limit should also be adopted.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Method Suitability > Calculating Endotoxin Limits for Drug and Biological Products

questions.topic: Prefilled syringe as a combination product
questions.question: For a combination product made up of a drug and a device, such as a prefilled syringe, how does the chapter recommend setting the endotoxin limit?

options.A: Evaluate the syringe separately against the medical device limit of 20 EU/device, and apply the drug limit to the drug separately
options.B: Test the syringe as the filled unit, and use the drug's endotoxin limit as the basis
options.C: Always apply 2.15 EU/device for devices contacting cerebrospinal fluid, because the syringe is a parenteral device
options.D: Take the more lenient of the drug limit and the device limit as the limit

questions.explanation: A prefilled syringe can be tested as the whole filled unit, and the drug's endotoxin limit takes precedence; the endotoxin contributed by the container (device) is considered to be extracted together with the drug during sample preparation and is already counted in the product's measurable endotoxin.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Method Suitability > Calculating Endotoxin Limits for Combination Products

questions.question: A product's endotoxin limit and starting concentration remain unchanged. The laboratory changes the method from gel-clot with labeled sensitivity λ = 0.25 EU/mL to a quantitative method whose lowest standard curve point is 0.05 EU/mL. How does the MVD change?

options.A: It falls to 1/5 of the original, because a more sensitive method leaves less room for dilution
options.B: It stays the same, because MVD depends only on the endotoxin limit and not on method sensitivity
options.C: It increases 5-fold, because the smaller the λ, the larger the MVD and the more room there is to dilute out interfering substances
options.D: It increases 25-fold, because MVD is inversely proportional to the square of the sensitivity rather than linearly related

questions.explanation: MVD = (endotoxin limit × product concentration) ÷ λ, so it is inversely proportional to λ. A drop in λ from 0.25 to 0.05 is a reduction to 1/5, so MVD increases 5-fold; a more sensitive method provides more dilution room to overcome product interference.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Method Suitability > Maximum Valid Dilution

questions.question: A product lot fails the endotoxin limit at the MVD dilution. To understand the actual level of contamination, what does the chapter recommend the laboratory do?

options.A: Dilute beyond the MVD to the endpoint (gel-clot negative or a valid quantitative reading) to learn the total content
options.B: Repeat the test several times at the MVD dilution and take the average as the final endotoxin content to make the decision directly
options.C: Heat the sample and add extra CSE until the PPC recovery falls within the acceptable range
options.D: Switch to a less sensitive lysate so that the result falls within the limit, then report again

questions.explanation: The MVD does not limit the dilution needed to learn the true level of contamination. The actual endotoxin content can be used for trend analysis and helps trace the root cause during an OOS investigation.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Method Suitability > Maximum Valid Dilution

questions.topic: Reading a vendor CoA for disposables
questions.question: The CoA supplied by the vendor states that a 10 mL dilution tube is "<0.5 EU/mL". If this result was obtained with 5 mL of extract, how should the endotoxin amount per tube be interpreted?

options.A: <0.5 EU/tube, because the stated concentration value already represents the total for the whole tube
options.B: <0.1 EU/tube, because the larger the extract volume, the lower the actual content per tube
options.C: <5 EU/tube, because this is the nominal tube capacity of 10 mL multiplied by the stated concentration
options.D: <2.5 EU/tube, because the volume actually used for extraction was 5 mL rather than the nominal capacity

questions.explanation: The chapter's example: a 1 mL extraction represents <0.5 EU/tube, a 5 mL extraction represents <2.5 EU/tube, and a 10 mL extraction represents <5 EU/tube. The laboratory therefore needs to confirm the extraction volume and BET conditions with the vendor and cannot rely on the label alone.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Preparatory Requirements > Screening and Qualification of Consumables: Compendial Requirement

questions.topic: Number of lots for suitability testing
questions.question: According to USP <1085>, how should the number of product lots used for BET method suitability testing be decided?

options.A: Always use three consecutive lots, which is the chapter's minimum requirement and may not be increased or decreased according to product characteristics
options.B: Decide in advance based on a risk assessment; products with high variability (such as biologics) usually need more than three lots
options.C: One lot is enough, because the <85> method is already considered validated and lot-to-lot differences need not be considered
options.D: It is needed only at the commercial stage; at the clinical stage there are few lots, so it need not be performed

questions.explanation: Three consecutive lots used to be considered enough, but the chapter recommends deciding the number of lots in advance and supporting it with a risk assessment (lifecycle stage, sources of variability, material testing history). The greater the variability of starting materials, API and process, the more lots than three are usually needed; where variability is very small, three lots are sufficient.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Method Suitability > Method Suitability Testing > interference screening for drug products

questions.question: The BET of a biologic is suspected of false positives caused by glucan interference. According to Table 3 of the chapter, which countermeasure should be preferred?

options.A: Use a glucan blocker supplied by the reagent manufacturer and specific to the method and lysate formulation used
options.B: Use a diluent containing 1 mM EDTA to chelate the divalent cations that interfere with the LAL reaction
options.C: Add a magnesium-containing buffer to prevent LPS aggregation and restore detection accuracy
options.D: Adjust the pH with endotoxin-free HCl or NaOH so that the lysate plus sample falls in the optimal range

questions.explanation: Glucan interferes with the LAL reaction, and the countermeasure is to use a glucan blocker supplied by the reagent manufacturer; because methods and lysate formulations differ, it should be used according to the manufacturer's instructions. EDTA is for heavy metals and calcium ions, magnesium-containing buffer is for chelating agents, and pH adjustment is for pH interference.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Method Suitability > Method Suitability Testing > common test interferences (Table 3)

questions.question: A small-volume injectable has an MVD of 240, and the laboratory decides to pool 3 vials into one sample for release testing. What should the adjusted MVD be?

options.A: 720, because the total volume increases after pooling, so a larger dilution can be used
options.B: 240, because pooling does not change the product's endotoxin limit, so the MVD does not change
options.C: 120, because simply halving the MVD compensates for the dilution effect of pooling
options.D: 80, which lowers the effective endotoxin limit to one third of the original to compensate for the dilution from pooling

questions.explanation: After pooling, the MVD must be divided by the number of units in the pool: 240 ÷ 3 = 80, to account for the possibility that only one unit contains endotoxin. This lowers the product's effective limit to one third.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Pooling

questions.question: Which of the following samples is least suitable for pooling?

options.A: Finished product vials from the same lot used for lot release testing, with scientific justification
options.B: A solution injectable with a high MVD and homogeneous contents, for which the MVD has been adjusted
options.C: In-process samples taken from the process that represent different manufacturing stages
options.D: Medical devices that are customarily combined into one extract and tested together

questions.explanation: The chapter states clearly that pooling is not applicable to in-process samples that represent different manufacturing stages. Pooling can be used for lot release testing, and medical devices are customarily pooled; suspensions with a low MVD or where homogeneity cannot be ensured are less suitable.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Pooling

questions.question: A product has a starting concentration of 10 mg/mL. After correction for the dilution factor, gel-clot gives 5 EU/mL of endotoxin. If the specification is expressed in EU/mg, what is the result?

options.A: 0.5 EU/mg, obtained by dividing EU/mL by the concentration in mg/mL
options.B: 2 EU/mg, obtained by dividing the concentration in mg/mL by EU/mL
options.C: 50 EU/mg, obtained by directly multiplying EU/mL by the concentration in mg/mL
options.D: 5 EU/mg, because the BET result unit is already EU/mg

questions.explanation: All BET results are reported in EU/mL; if the specification is in EU/mg, EU/mL must be divided by the concentration: 5 EU/mL ÷ 10 mg/mL = 0.5 EU/mg.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Calculation of Endotoxin Content

questions.question: The standard curve of a kinetic quantitative BET has a correlation coefficient of |r| = 0.979. According to USP <1085>, how should this curve be handled?

options.A: Acceptable, because rounded to two decimal places it is 0.98, which meets the requirement
options.B: Not acceptable, because the requirement is |r| ≥ 0.980 and it cannot be made to pass by rounding
options.C: Acceptable, as long as the slope is negative and the curve is within the range recommended by the reagent
options.D: Not acceptable, because the linearity requirement for quantitative BET is |r| ≥ 0.990

questions.explanation: The linearity requirement for all compendial quantitative BETs is |r| ≥ 0.980, and it is written to three significant figures because the final "0" matters, so 0.979 cannot be rounded up. In addition, an acceptable r does not guarantee that there is no dilution error.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Standard Curve Control

questions.topic: Catching a dilution error in standards
questions.question: While preparing the standards, an analyst accidentally diluted them an extra two-fold, but the correlation coefficient of the standard curve still meets |r| ≥ 0.980. Where is this error most likely to show up?

options.A: The correlation coefficient r would drop clearly below 0.980, so it is immediately judged a failure
options.B: The onset or reaction time of the standards would become shorter, because the lower concentration makes the reaction occur faster
options.C: The onset or reaction time of the standards becomes longer and the y-intercept also deviates; r alone would not reveal it
options.D: It would leave no trace; it could be noticed only by remaking the standards and comparing the new and old curves

questions.explanation: A dilution error can still give a well-linear standard curve, which r alone cannot reveal; an over-diluted standard reacts more slowly (a longer onset time), which is also reflected in the y-intercept. The onset times of standards should therefore be monitored across runs, instruments and analysts.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Standard Curve Control

questions.question: A product lot's BET result exceeds the limit, but review shows that the negative control in that test gave a reaction. How should this result be classified?

options.A: An OOS result, because the sample result is out of specification, so a Phase II investigation must be started directly
options.B: An OOS result, but because the negative control is abnormal, the result may be averaged with earlier tests before deciding
options.C: Still a valid result, because as long as the sample result exceeds the limit, an abnormal control does not matter
options.D: An invalid test rather than an OOS, which still must be tracked and trended to find whether any pattern needs correction

questions.explanation: When system suitability parameters (such as the negative control, PPC, gel-clot labeled sensitivity confirmation, linear standard curve) are not as expected, the test is invalid and is not an OOS. A true OOS exists only when a valid test gives an out-of-specification result, but invalid tests should still be tracked and trended.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Out-of-Specification Results and Retesting Considerations

questions.topic: Phase I vs Phase II investigation
questions.question: When an OOS occurs in the BET, what is the difference between a Phase I and a Phase II investigation?

options.A: Phase I is a laboratory investigation confirming the accuracy of the original result; Phase II addresses production operations and should be conducted by a cross-functional team
options.B: Phase I addresses production operations and facilities; Phase II is a laboratory investigation in which QC personnel confirm the original result
options.C: Both phases are conducted within the laboratory; the only difference is that in Phase II the vendor must additionally retest the sample
options.D: Phase I is performed before the OOS is confirmed; Phase II is performed only at the retest stage after an OOS result has been obtained

questions.explanation: Phase I is a laboratory investigation aimed at confirming the accuracy of the original test result (sampling, sample preparation, reagents, instruments, calculations, analysts, etc.). Phase II is an investigation of production operations, re-evaluating validated process controls, and is usually carried out by a cross-functional team including operations, facilities, engineering and microbiology experts.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Out-of-Specification Results and Retesting Considerations

questions.topic: Investigational testing is not a retest
questions.question: During an OOS investigation, the laboratory performs one more investigational test on the original sample preparation, and the result meets the specification. Can the lot be released on this basis?

options.A: Yes, because the passing second result is enough to overturn the original OOS result
options.B: Yes, as long as the two results are averaged and the average falls within the specification range
options.C: No, investigational testing is not a retest; its purpose is to find the cause and confirm whether there was really an error
options.D: Yes, as long as the QA head gives verbal agreement on site and the investigation record is completed afterwards

questions.explanation: The chapter states that investigational testing is not considered a retest and should not be used to release material; it is used to test hypotheses and find conditions that may have caused test inaccuracy. If the second result passes, there may still be an error in the original or second test, so further hypotheses must be proposed and confirmed. Investigational testing should be approved in advance and fully documented.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Out-of-Specification Results and Retesting Considerations

questions.topic: Misreading the gel-clot final decision statement
questions.question: <85> contains the sentence "in the event of doubt or dispute, the final decision is made on the basis of the gel-clot limit test". A laboratory's routine method (a kinetic method) gives an OOS, but gel-clot gives a pass. Can the laboratory cite this sentence to claim the lot passes?

options.A: Yes, because gel-clot is the original method and its result always takes precedence over other methods
options.B: No, this sentence applies only to the specific situation in which a regulatory authority and a laboratory use different platforms and their results conflict
options.C: Yes, as long as the customer is notified first and the report states that the result is from a gel-clot limit test
options.D: No, because gel-clot is no longer a compendially recognized BET method, so its result is always invalid

questions.explanation: This sentence is often misunderstood. It applies only when a regulatory agency uses gel-clot for release testing and the testing laboratory uses another BET platform and the results conflict; it does not allow a laboratory to switch to a passing gel-clot result when its routine method gives an OOS. Gel-clot itself is still a method recognized in <85>.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Routine Testing > Out-of-Specification Results and Retesting Considerations

questions.question: A laboratory wants to adopt an endotoxin detection method not listed in <85> (for example, another platform). According to USP <1085>, what is required?

options.A: Because the BET itself is considered validated, an alternate method needs only to be notified to the regulatory authority afterwards
options.B: It needs only suitability testing with three product lots showing no interference before the method is formally adopted
options.C: It needs only agreement with the results on the vendor's CoA to replace the original compendial method
options.D: It must be fully validated, showing that decisions are equivalent to or better than with the compendial method, and approved by the regulatory authority

questions.explanation: The methods listed in <85> are considered validated, but if a method not listed is adopted, it must be fully validated to ensure that decisions made on that basis are equivalent to or better than with the compendial method, and ultimately approved by the appropriate regulatory authority; <1223> and <1225> can guide the validation approach.
questions.reference: USP <1085> Alternate Test Methods
